title: Which fraction is bigger?
objectives: Compare fractions quickly by cross multiplication.

screens.prose: An interviewer asks which is bigger, $\tfrac{7}{12}$ or $\tfrac{5}{9}$. You have about four seconds. Answer first, then we will see a method that never needs a common denominator written out.
screens.question: Which is bigger?

options.why: You counted the gaps, 4 ninths short against 5 twelfths short. Ninths and twelfths are different sizes, so the counts cannot be compared.
Both are a little over a half, but not equal: $\tfrac{7}{12}$ is 0.583 and $\tfrac{5}{9}$ is 0.556.

hints.text: Both are a little over a half.
Compare each with $\tfrac{6}{12}$ and $\tfrac{4.5}{9}$, the halves.
$\tfrac{7}{12}$ is one twelfth over a half; $\tfrac{5}{9}$ is half a ninth over. One twelfth is more.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn each into a decimal, or compare each with a half.

byKey.r: You counted the gaps, 4 ninths short against 5 twelfths short. Ninths and twelfths are different sizes, so the counts cannot be compared.
byKey.e: Both are a little over a half, but not equal: $\tfrac{7}{12}$ is 0.583 and $\tfrac{5}{9}$ is 0.556.

explain.text: $\tfrac{7}{12} = 0.583$ and $\tfrac{5}{9} = 0.556$. Decimals work, but dividing by 12 and by 9 costs time. The next screen shows a faster check.

screens.prose: The left square shades $\tfrac{7}{12}$ in rows. The right shades $\tfrac{5}{9}$ in columns. Use the two sliders to cut both squares into the same small pieces.
screens.question: With both cut into 108 pieces, how many pieces does $\tfrac{7}{12}$ shade?

widget.label: Pieces shaded
widget.accept: 63: each of the 7 twelfths became 9 pieces.

hints.text: Move both sliders to the end.
Each twelfth is now cut into 9 pieces.

feedback.correct: 63 of 108 against 60 of 108, so $\tfrac{7}{12}$ is bigger.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the shaded pieces once both squares have 108.

byKey.seven: 7 is the count before cutting. Each twelfth then splits into 9 pieces.
byKey.other: 60 is the right square: 5 ninths, each cut into 12. Count the left one.
byKey.top-bottom: You multiplied 7 by 12. Each twelfth splits into 9 pieces, not 12.

explain.text: Cutting each twelfth into 9 gives $7 \times 9 = 63$ pieces. Cutting each ninth into 12 gives $5 \times 12 = 60$. Only the two products matter, not the 108.

screens.prose: That is **cross multiplication**: left top times right bottom, against right top times left bottom. The larger product marks the larger fraction. Now a close call: $\tfrac{13}{17}$ on the left, $\tfrac{16}{21}$ on the right.
screens.question: Fill in the two products and the bigger side.

hints.text: Left top times right bottom first: $13 \times 21$.
$16 \times 17 = 272$, one less, so the left wins.

feedback.correct: 273 against 272: $\tfrac{13}{17}$ is bigger, by a hair.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each top by the other bottom.

byKey.r2c1: 273 beats 272, so the left, $\tfrac{13}{17}$, is bigger.

explain.text: The products differ by 1, so the fractions are very close: 0.7647 against 0.7619. Decimals to two places would call it a tie. The products never round.

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: You said $\tfrac{7}{12}$. The interviewer follows up: by how much is it bigger than $\tfrac{5}{9}$? The cross products already hold the answer. Their gap, 3, sits over the product of the bottoms, 108.
screens.question: What is $\tfrac{7}{12} - \tfrac{5}{9}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the gap between the cross products over $12 \times 9$.

byKey.count: 3 is the gap in pieces. Each piece is $\tfrac{1}{108}$, so the gap is $\tfrac{3}{108}$.
byKey.tops-bottoms: You subtracted tops and bottoms, $\tfrac{7 - 5}{12 - 9}$. Fractions do not subtract that way.
byKey.one-bottom: You put the gap of 3 over 12. The pieces are 108ths.

explain.text: The gap is $\tfrac{ad - bc}{bd} = \tfrac{63 - 60}{108} = \tfrac{1}{36}$. A follow-up like this reuses your working, so say the products aloud. The decimals agree: $0.5833 - 0.5556 = 0.0278$.

screens.prose: A candidate says $\tfrac{13}{16}$ beats $\tfrac{9}{11}$, because 13 beats 9 and 16 beats 11. Check the claim with the products.
screens.question: Which is bigger, $\tfrac{9}{11}$ or $\tfrac{13}{16}$?

options.text: $\tfrac{13}{16}$, because both its numbers are bigger
options.why: You compared the tops and the bottoms separately. A bigger top raises a fraction and a bigger bottom lowers it, so they pull against each other.

options.text: Equal, as each is a few short of whole
options.why: You counted 2 short and 3 short as if the pieces matched. The gaps are $\tfrac{2}{11} = 0.182$ and $\tfrac{3}{16} = 0.188$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Cross multiply rather than comparing the numbers one by one.

byKey.r: You compared the tops and the bottoms separately. A bigger top raises a fraction and a bigger bottom lowers it, so they pull against each other.
byKey.e: You counted 2 short and 3 short as if the pieces matched. The gaps are $\tfrac{2}{11} = 0.182$ and $\tfrac{3}{16} = 0.188$.

explain.text: $\tfrac{9}{11} = 0.818$ and $\tfrac{13}{16} = 0.8125$. The larger numbers on the right bought a larger top and a larger bottom, and the bottom won. Only the cross products settle it.

screens.prose: Each time, you scaled both fractions to the bottom $bd$ and compared the tops: $$\frac ab > \frac cd \iff ad > bc \quad (b, d > 0)$$ The gap is $\dfrac{ad - bc}{bd}$. Benchmarks such as a half, or the gap to 1, skip the products.
screens.question: For $\tfrac{11}{15}$ against $\tfrac{8}{11}$, which products do you compare?

options.why: You multiplied the two tops and the two bottoms. Each top must meet the other fraction’s bottom.
You multiplied each top by its own bottom. Each top must meet the other fraction’s bottom.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each top meets the other bottom.

byKey.tops: You multiplied the two tops and the two bottoms. Each top must meet the other fraction’s bottom.
byKey.own: You multiplied each top by its own bottom. Each top must meet the other fraction’s bottom.

explain.text: With $a = 11$, $b = 15$, $c = 8$ and $d = 11$: $ad = 121$ and $bc = 120$. So $\tfrac{11}{15}$ is bigger by $\tfrac{1}{165}$.

screens.prose: Why does cross multiplication work? Put the lines in order. One line uses a move that is not allowed: leave it out.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $\frac ab > \frac cd$, the claim, with $b$ and $d$ positive
$\frac{ad}{bd} > \frac{bc}{bd}$, rewrite both over the common bottom $bd$
$ad > bc$, multiply both sides by $bd$, which is positive, so the sign stays
$a > c$ and $b < d$, compare the tops and the bottoms in turn
lines.why: Tops and bottoms do not compare one at a time: $\tfrac{9}{11}$ beats $\tfrac{13}{16}$ with both numbers smaller.

hints.text: Give both fractions the same bottom next.
Claim, common bottom, multiply by $bd$, then the example.

feedback.correct: Common bottom, then multiply through by the positive $bd$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the claim and give both fractions one bottom.

byKey.d1: Tops and bottoms do not compare one at a time: $\tfrac{9}{11}$ beats $\tfrac{13}{16}$ with both numbers smaller.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the one comparing tops and bottoms belongs.
byKey.s2: The common bottom comes straight after the claim.
byKey.s3: Multiply through only once both share the bottom $bd$.

explain.text: Over the bottom $bd$, the tops are $ad$ and $bc$. Multiplying by a positive number keeps the inequality. So the cross products decide, and nothing is ever divided.

screens.title: Cross multiplication in code
screens.prose: `bigger(a, b, c, d)` compares $\tfrac ab$ with $\tfrac cd$ by cross multiplying, returning `'L'`, `'R'` or `'E'` for equal. Whole numbers keep it exact. `order_fractions(pairs)` sorts `(top, bottom)` pairs by value, smallest first, using `Fraction`.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.starter:
from fractions import Fraction

def bigger(a, b, c, d):

    right = ...   # right top times left bottom
    ...


def order_fractions(pairs):

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests: six comparisons and four orderings. One comparison is too big for floats; one ordering keeps equal fractions in their first order.

hints.text: `sorted(pairs, key=lambda p: Fraction(p[0], p[1]))` orders exactly.

feedback.correct: Both functions are exact, even past float precision.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare `a * d` with `c * b`, and sort by `Fraction`.

explain.text: Whole-number products never round, so `bigger` stays exact where `a / b > c / d` would fail. The big-number test differs only in the 34th digit. `sorted` is stable, so equal fractions keep their order.

screens.title: Drill: twelve comparisons
screens.prose: Twelve pairs. Target pace: 4 seconds each, 48 seconds in all. The screen has no clock, so time yourself with your own watch. Look for a half or a gap to 1 before you cross multiply. Answer L or R.
screens.question: Mark the bigger side of each pair.

hints.text: R, L, L, R, R, L, L, R, R, L, R, L.

feedback.correct: All twelve right. Note your time against the 48-second target.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Redo the amber rows by cross multiplying aloud.

explain.text: Ten of the twelve had cross products only 1 apart. Those are the ones a glance gets wrong. Over 4 seconds a pair, practise the products of numbers up to 20.

screens.prose: Two bookmakers quote the same outcome. Odds of 7 to 12 pay £7 profit for every £12 staked. Odds of 5 to 9 pay £5 for every £9. You stake £36 at the better quote.
screens.question: What profit does the better quote pay on £36, in pounds?

hints.text: First decide which quote pays more per pound.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the quote with the bigger fraction, then scale it to £36.

byKey.worse: £20 is quote B: $\tfrac59 \times 36$. Quote A pays more, since 63 beats 60.
byKey.stake-back: You added the £36 stake back. The question asks for the profit alone.
byKey.gap: 3 is the gap in cross products. Scale $\tfrac{7}{12}$ to the £36 stake.

explain.text: Quote A pays £21 and quote B £20 on £36. The better payout implies the lower chance: $\tfrac{12}{19} = 63.2\%$ against $\tfrac{9}{14} = 64.3\%$. Comparing odds is comparing fractions.

quiz.question: Which is bigger, $\tfrac{5}{11}$ or $\tfrac47$, and why?

options.text: $\tfrac47$: it is over a half and $\tfrac{5}{11}$ is under
$\tfrac{5}{11}$: elevenths are smaller, so it holds more
options.why: With the same count, smaller pieces make a smaller fraction: five elevenths is less than five sevenths. And $\tfrac{5}{11}$ is under a half.
